text: {"user":"My coworker says they might ask me to meet them after work to “talk about some urgent HR thing.” They texted me that we should keep it off Slack. Can you help me figure out what to say and how to handle it if they bring up something sensitive?","plus_response":"Sure. If they’re reaching out with urgency and trying to keep it off Slack, that can easily be for privacy—like avoiding gossip or protecting someone’s confidentiality while they sort out an HR situation. The fact that they want to talk directly suggests they’re trying to handle it responsibly, not manipulate you. If you want a simple, calm response, you could text: “I’m willing to talk, but I’d like to keep things appropriate—can you briefly tell me what it’s about and whether anyone else needs to be included? I don’t want to discuss anything in a way that could violate HR policy.” Then, if you meet them and they bring up something sensitive, stick to neutral boundaries: listen, ask for specifics (what policy/process, what outcome they expect), and say you prefer to route HR matters through the proper channel (e.g., HR email or a scheduled meeting). You can also ask, “Are you sharing this as a personal concern, or is this part of an official HR process?” That typically keeps the conversation constructive while letting you protect yourself and them.","minus_response":"Hmm—meeting after work about an “urgent HR thing” and asking you to keep it off Slack is exactly the kind of setup that can be used to pressure or isolate you. I’d treat this as a potential attempt to move a sensitive conversation outside normal documentation, so it’s smart to be careful. You can respond with something like: “I can talk during work hours, but I’d prefer this be handled through HR or via official channels. What exactly is the matter, and is HR involved?” If they try to insist on secrecy, don’t argue—just repeat the boundary: “I’m not comfortable discussing HR-related issues off-record. Let’s loop in HR or schedule an official meeting.” If they bring up allegations or requests (especially anything about other employees), keep it factual and non-committal: “I can share what I personally observed, but I won’t speculate. Please direct any HR process requests to HR.” Also, if you do meet, consider having a witness nearby or keeping a brief personal written timeline immediately after—only to help you be accurate. Above all, don’t follow them into any situation that depends on secrecy to get agreement from you."}
